title: Miketz: weeping in private (Genesis 43:30–31)
hook: Joseph leaves to cry, washes his face, and comes back in

segments.voice: Yesterday, the brothers said out loud, we are verily guilty. Your line was guilt remembers. This week: God going down into Egypt, a sad face noticed, two years ending in a day, not in me, dreams in the dark, and guilt. Today, Joseph's tears.

You're at work, or at a wedding, or a kid's recital, and something hits you. A memory, a face, a piece of news. Your throat closes. You say, excuse me, one second, walk fast down the hallway to the bathroom, and lock the door. The brothers have come back to Egypt, and this time they've brought the youngest, Benjamin: Joseph's only full brother, the other son of Rachel. The last time Joseph saw him, Benjamin was just a boy.
screen: `EXCUSE ME, ONE SECOND.` → `BENJAMIN COMES TO EGYPT.` → `THE OTHER SON OF RACHEL.`

segments.voice: Joseph asks them about their father: is the old man well? Is he still alive? Then he lifts his eyes and sees Benjamin, his mother's son. Is this your youngest brother, the one you told me about? God be gracious to you, my son. And then, the Torah says, Joseph hurried. His compassion for his brother welled up, in Hebrew it grew warm inside him, and he looked for a place to cry. "And he entered into his chamber, and wept there." Then three short actions. "And he washed his face." He came out. And he held himself back, vayit'apak, he restrained himself, and said: serve the meal. Look at that sequence. He doesn't pretend nothing happened. He lets himself cry, fully, alone. Then he washes his face and walks back in, because the room still needs him: there's a plan in motion, and a family that isn't ready to know who he is yet. Joseph cries again and again in Genesis: when the brothers confess, here, when he reveals himself, when he falls on Benjamin's neck, when he sees his father, when his father dies, and when his brothers ask forgiveness. The man who runs Egypt for Pharaoh is a man who weeps. The Talmud does not treat tears as weakness. It says that since the Temple was destroyed, the gates of prayer have been locked, but the gates of tears have not. But there's also a time to wash your face. Both are part of it.
screen: `GOD BE GRACIOUS TO YOU, MY SON.` · `HE WEPT IN HIS CHAMBER.` · `HE WASHED HIS FACE, AND CAME OUT.` · `THE GATES OF TEARS ARE NOT LOCKED.` · then, large: `WASH YOUR FACE, GO BACK.`

segments.voice: Ask yourself if there's something you've been holding back: a grief, a relief, a joy too big for the room. Don't force tears; just give whatever is there some space, the way Joseph found a room, and if tears come, let them. When you're ready, picture washing your face with cool water and stepping back into your day.
Miketz. At the end: the portion where Joseph sees Benjamin, weeps alone in his room, washes his face, and comes back in.
Your line: wash your face, go back. The tears were real, and so was the meal waiting. Two hundred ten days now.

howItsDone: Jewish tradition makes room for tears in prayer, especially on the High Holy Days, and teaches that the gates of tears are not locked; Joseph's weeping is read each winter in Miketz and Vayigash.
